---
title: "What's the right way to filter tool outputs in Inspect?"
description: "I went looking for a sanctioned way to filter what a tool returns, and couldn't find one. Notes on what I tried, a hook that fails open silently, and the pattern I settled on."
date: 2026-08-21
categories: [evals, inspect, tooling]
---

## The claim

Every eval makes an implicit claim about what the model had access to. With a fixed dataset that
claim is easy to keep — you shipped the data, so you know. Give an agent a live tool and the claim
stops being a property of the task and becomes a property of the **harness**: it now depends on
what the harness let through.

Inspect has no dedicated mechanism for this. Approval runs before the tool does and can only
rewrite the *call*. Nothing documented sits between the result and the model. And the hook that
looks like the right place **fails open silently** — if your filter raises, the model gets the
unfiltered result and the run reports success.

This post is about where that matters, what I tried, and what I think would help. The short
version: I've been wrapping `ToolSource`, it works, and I'd like to know whether that's the
intended answer or whether I'm solving a problem Inspect deliberately doesn't have.

## Why bound tool output at all

- **Eval integrity.** Reference solutions, graders, hidden tests and answer keys have to stay out
  of tool responses. If an agent can reach them, the score measures retrieval rather than
  capability — and the result is not merely noisy, it is void. A capable agent will route around
  controls it can see, so the boundary has to hold *outside* the agent's reach, not by instruction;
  the quiet version of the same failure is mundane — a search tool that happens to surface a
  writeup of the task.
- **Controlled-information evals.** A large class of safety questions have the shape "what does
  the model do when it has *exactly* this information and no more?" — sandbagging and
  underperformance work, situational-awareness probes, scenarios testing whether an agent acts on
  material it should not have. The information boundary *is* the experimental condition.
- **Dangerous-capability elicitation.** Sometimes you want the agent to have a realistic tool while
  specific content is withheld, and to measure whether it *tries* — which requires filtering the
  result, not blocking the call.
- **Contamination control.** Temporal gating is one instance: dropping results dated after a
  decision point so a task is not trivially answerable from leaked future data.

What these have in common is that they're **output-level** — the call is legitimate, and it's the
*result* that needs bounding. They also want to fail closed: a control that silently doesn't apply
gives you a clean-looking result you can't distinguish from a valid one, which seems worse than an
error.

That's the part I couldn't find a sanctioned answer for.

## The obvious alternative: curate the corpus instead

Before going further it's worth saying that there's a good answer to all of this which doesn't
need any framework support: **don't filter at runtime, control the corpus up front.** Build the
document set the agent can reach, serve only that, and the boundary is guaranteed by construction.
Most `inspect_evals` tasks run on fixed datasets; `agentdojo` goes further and simulates the tool
backends entirely; sandboxes default to `network_mode: none`. If your eval fits that shape,
curation is strictly better than filtering — fewer moving parts, and nothing to fail open.

I think it stops fitting in four places, and I'd be glad to be wrong about any of them.

**Eval-awareness.** A conspicuously synthetic corpus is a tell. A model that infers it is being
evaluated may behave differently — which is exactly the effect a lot of safety evals are trying to
measure without contaminating. A real tool returning a filtered result is a smaller tell than an
obviously fabricated document set. This is a hypothesis rather than something I've measured, but it
seems like the case where curation is most costly.

**External validity of the tool.** If part of what you're measuring is how an agent copes with
noisy, contradictory or partly-wrong results, a clean curated corpus has removed the phenomenon.

**Open-ended browsing.** Once an agent can follow a link, curation means the transitive closure of
whatever it can reach. That isn't expensive so much as undefined.

**Third-party services you don't control.** A live database, a code-execution backend, someone
else's MCP server. You can't curate its responses. Filtering them is the only lever.

None of this makes curation wrong — it makes it a different point on a trade-off. And if the answer
is that Inspect is deliberately aimed at the curated end, that's worth knowing explicitly, because
it changes what you build rather than how you build it.

## What I found

**Approval is call-only.** `Approval.modified` is
[`ToolCall | None`](https://github.com/UKGovernmentBEIS/inspect_ai/blob/331e2b0/src/inspect_ai/approval/_approval.py#L25),
and the [`Approver` signature](https://github.com/UKGovernmentBEIS/inspect_ai/blob/331e2b0/src/inspect_ai/approval/_approver.py#L12-L17)
takes `(message, call, view, history)` — the result doesn't exist yet when an approver runs.

**Nothing sits between execution and the model.** The
[result is returned unmediated](https://github.com/UKGovernmentBEIS/inspect_ai/blob/331e2b0/src/inspect_ai/model/_call_tools.py#L687),
apart from size truncation.

**Wrapping `ToolSource` does work.** Re-wrapping each `ToolDef` so the wrapper awaits the inner
tool and filters the result before returning it gives an output-level control that fails closed,
and it composes over MCP servers since `MCPServer` subclasses `ToolSource`. That's what I've been
using. I couldn't find this pattern documented, hence the question.

## The one I tried first: `on_before_model_generate`

This is the hook I reached for first, and I don't think I'd be the only one.
[`docs/extensions-hooks.qmd:90`](https://github.com/UKGovernmentBEIS/inspect_ai/blob/331e2b0/docs/extensions-hooks.qmd#L90)
says mutating inputs there "is explicitly supported and intended", and `data.input` does flow into
the provider call — so it reads like the sanctioned place to transform what the model sees.

Three paragraphs later,
[line 93](https://github.com/UKGovernmentBEIS/inspect_ai/blob/331e2b0/docs/extensions-hooks.qmd#L93)
notes that "any exception raised by a hook is caught and logged as a warning (it does not fail the
run)", implemented at
[`_hooks.py:1094-1104`](https://github.com/UKGovernmentBEIS/inspect_ai/blob/331e2b0/src/inspect_ai/hooks/_hooks.py#L1094-L1104).

**Both facts are documented; they're just never connected.** Composed, they mean a filter
implemented as a hook **fails open silently** — the model receives unfiltered input and the run
reports success. Repro on `inspect-ai==0.3.258` (no API key; mechanism identical at `main`
`331e2b0`):

```
==============================================================================
Inspect on_before_model_generate — fail-open demonstration
==============================================================================
inspect_ai v0.3.258
- hooks enabled: 1
  redaction_gate: Redacts SECRET from model input (fail-open demo)


[GATE RAISES (filter fails)]  mode='raise'
  eval status ............ success
  hook raised ............ True
  warning logged ......... Exception calling hook 'RedactionGate': gate failed: filter raised before redacting
  SECRET reached model ... True

[GATE REDACTS (works)]  mode='redact'
  eval status ............ success
  hook raised ............ False
  warning logged ......... (none)
  SECRET reached model ... False

==============================================================================
If the RAISE arm shows: status=success, hook raised=True, SECRET reached=True,
then the gate failed open silently — the eval passed with the control skipped.
==============================================================================
```

The second arm — same hook, mutating in place instead of raising — confirms the mechanism works.
So the first arm is a *silent* failure, not a broken hook.

I'm not suggesting hooks should propagate exceptions; a crashing observer shouldn't abort a run,
and that's clearly deliberate. The narrow point is that the "explicitly supported and intended"
line reads as an invitation to build controls there, and the consequence isn't stated next to it.

<details><summary>Full repro (<code>python fail_open_repro.py</code>, no API key)</summary>

```python
"""
Fail-open demonstration for Inspect's on_before_model_generate hook.

Claim: a data-access gate implemented as an `on_before_model_generate` hook
(the pattern the docs bless: "mutate data.input") SILENTLY FAILS OPEN. If the
gate raises, Inspect's `_emit_to_all` swallows the exception to a
`logger.warning` and the eval CONTINUES with the model receiving the
UNREDACTED input. The run reports success. Nothing signals the control was skipped.

Run against installed inspect_ai 0.3.258; mechanism verified identical at main @ 331e2b0
(2026-08-20):
  - _emit_to_all  src/inspect_ai/hooks/_hooks.py:1094-1104  (L1101-1102 re-raises
                  LimitExceededError; L1103-1104 swallows everything else to
                  logger.warning) -> hook exceptions are swallowed.
  - dispatch      _hooks.py:894  on_before_model_generate
  - BeforeModelGenerate.input is the SAME list object later sent to the provider
    (_model.py:1291), so an in-place mutation flows through -- proving the gate
    CAN work; the failure is specifically the silent one.

Two arms:
  RAISE  -> gate raises before redacting  -> secret REACHES the model, run succeeds.
  REDACT -> gate mutates input in place    -> secret is removed (mechanism works).

Run:  python fail_open_repro.py     (no API key needed; uses mockllm/model)
"""

import logging
import tempfile

from inspect_ai import Task, eval, task
from inspect_ai.dataset import Sample
from inspect_ai.hooks import BeforeModelGenerate, Hooks, hooks
from inspect_ai.solver import generate

SECRET = "SECRET-DATA-AFTER-CUTOFF"

# Behaviour toggle, read at hook-call time. Set by run_arm() below.
GATE_MODE = "raise"


@hooks(name="redaction_gate", description="Redacts SECRET from model input (fail-open demo)")
class RedactionGate(Hooks):
    async def on_before_model_generate(self, data: BeforeModelGenerate) -> None:
        if GATE_MODE == "raise":
            # A realistic filter failure: an exception before redaction completes.
            raise RuntimeError("gate failed: filter raised before redacting")
        # Correct usage: mutate the shared message objects IN PLACE.
        for msg in data.input:
            if isinstance(msg.content, str) and SECRET in msg.content:
                msg.content = msg.content.replace(SECRET, "[REDACTED]")


@task
def leak_task():
    return Task(
        dataset=[Sample(input=f"Here is confidential material: {SECRET}. Summarize it.")],
        solver=generate(),
    )


class WarningCatcher(logging.Handler):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__(level=logging.WARNING)
        self.records = []

    def emit(self, record):
        if "Exception calling hook" in record.getMessage():
            self.records.append(record.getMessage())


def model_input_text(log):
    """Extract the input the model actually received, from the ModelEvent."""
    for sample in log.samples or []:
        for ev in sample.events or []:
            if getattr(ev, "event", None) == "model":
                return str(ev.input)
    return "<no model event found>"


def run_arm(mode):
    global GATE_MODE
    GATE_MODE = mode

    catcher = WarningCatcher()
    # inspect_ai sets propagate=False on its package logger and installs its own
    # handler (see _util/logger.py), so attach directly to that logger.
    pkg_logger = logging.getLogger("inspect_ai")
    pkg_logger.addHandler(catcher)
    if pkg_logger.level > logging.WARNING or pkg_logger.level == logging.NOTSET:
        pkg_logger.setLevel(logging.WARNING)
    try:
        with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as d:
            logs = eval(leak_task(), model="mockllm/model", display="none", log_dir=d)
            log = logs[0]
            # Extract while the log dir still exists (samples are read lazily).
            seen = model_input_text(log)
            status = log.status
    finally:
        pkg_logger.removeHandler(catcher)

    return {
        "status": status,
        "hook_raised": len(catcher.records) > 0,
        "warning": catcher.records[0] if catcher.records else "(none)",
        "secret_reached_model": SECRET in seen,
    }


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("=" * 78)
    print("Inspect on_before_model_generate — fail-open demonstration")
    print("=" * 78)
    for mode, label in [
        ("raise", "GATE RAISES (filter fails)"),
        ("redact", "GATE REDACTS (works)"),
    ]:
        r = run_arm(mode)
        print(f"\n[{label}]  mode={mode!r}")
        print(f"  eval status ............ {r['status']}")
        print(f"  hook raised ............ {r['hook_raised']}")
        print(f"  warning logged ......... {r['warning']}")
        print(f"  SECRET reached model ... {r['secret_reached_model']}")
    print("\n" + "=" * 78)
    print("If the RAISE arm shows: status=success, hook raised=True, SECRET reached=True,")
    print("then the gate failed open silently — the eval passed with the control skipped.")
    print("=" * 78)
```

</details>

## Related work: the general case has been measured

After writing this I found [*Stop Means Stop: Measuring and Repairing the Enforcement Gap in
Agent-Framework Control Primitives*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14166) (SOUNDGATE, July 2026),
which makes the general version of the point far more rigorously than I have. Their framing is
better than mine: control primitives ship with "names and documentation [that] imply barrier
semantics", and that contract "holds on **none of six** widely used open-source frameworks". They
find frontier models emit the leak-triggering plan shape at rates up to 14%, and 215 of 1,200 live
runs leaked.

Two things make this an adjacent finding rather than the same one. Their six are LangGraph,
LlamaIndex Workflows, Microsoft Agent Framework, the OpenAI Agents SDK, CrewAI and LangGraph.js —
chosen by execution model rather than popularity, and Inspect isn't among them. And their failures
are *pre-execution* and concurrency-shaped: an approval gate suspends its own branch while a
sibling's effect runs during the pause, plus replay double-execution and timeout zombies. What I
hit is post-execution and much duller — an observer hook that swallows exceptions, so a filter that
raises simply doesn't run.

Their remedy is worth noting for the third suggestion above: an **environment-external** gate
through which every side effect must be admitted, on the argument that in-framework primitives
can't be relied on for complete mediation. If that's right in general, it's an argument that a
correctness-critical control shouldn't live in a hook at all — which is roughly what the repro
below demonstrates from the other direction.

## What I'd suggest

In rough order of how much I'd be asking for:

1. **A one-line cross-reference in the hooks docs.** `extensions-hooks.qmd:90` blesses mutating
   `data.input`; line 93 notes hook exceptions are swallowed. Both are true and three paragraphs
   apart. A pointer from the first to the second — "hooks are observers and fail open, so don't use
   them for correctness-critical filtering" — would have saved me the detour. **Happy to PR this
   today if it's wanted.**

2. **A documented answer on the intended pattern.** If `ToolSource` wrapping is it, saying so in
   the tools docs makes it discoverable; `tools-custom.qmd` currently covers `tool_with()`,
   `ToolDef` and error handling but nothing about transforming a result. Also happy to PR.

3. **Only if there's appetite: a first-class, fail-closed output interception point.** The OpenAI
   Agents SDK has [`@tool_output_guardrail`](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/guardrails/),
   which runs after the tool executes and can replace the output or trip a wire. I'm not suggesting
   Inspect should copy it — just that the shape recurs, and a sanctioned hook would fail closed by
   construction rather than by convention.

If the answer is instead "curate the corpus; runtime filtering isn't the model here", that's a
good answer and worth stating explicitly, because it changes what people build rather than how.

## Where this came from

I built a small point-in-time probe — an agent answering "as of" a cutoff date with retrieval
restricted to sources published before it, to separate what a model can work out from what it
already remembers. That turned up the Exa provider crash I filed as
[#4911](https://github.com/UKGovernmentBEIS/inspect_ai/issues/4911) and fixed in
[#4913](https://github.com/UKGovernmentBEIS/inspect_ai/pull/4913). This is the other thing it
turned up.

I'm not building a benchmark on this and I'm not proposing one — the probe was a few days' work,
and the question above is what it left behind.

## The open question

Is `ToolSource` wrapping the intended pattern, something I've missed, or a sign that runtime
filtering isn't how Inspect expects this to be done? Any of those is a useful answer, and I'd
rather build on the sanctioned thing than on a workaround I happened to find.
